lessons: LESSON: before building a serve-layer adapter for a rail whose naming resembles an existing sibling group (setbackRules alongside setbackFrontFt/SideFt/RearFt/CornerFt), query the LIVE cell shape directly -- do not infer the shape from the sibling files' pattern. setbackRules turned out to be a companion-row rail while all four of its Ft-suffixed siblings are plain scalars; the naming proximity would have led straight to a wrong, silently-broken adapter (reading a permanently-null cell.value) that every one of its own unit tests could still have been written to pass, had the fixtures been hand-invented instead of live-sampled.

LESSON: a file's established `let`-then-Promise.all-destructuring-reassignment pattern (used so a catch block can still see partially-resolved variables) requires every destructured name to be pre-declared above the try block -- adding a name to the destructuring array and the response object without also adding its `let` declaration is a real, typecheck-catchable bug, not a style nit. Caught here only because tsc --noEmit was run before considering the lane done, not from visual review of a 1000+-line file.

LESSON: gh pr checks --watch (not a hand-rolled polling loop against gh pr checks' text output) is the correct tool for waiting on PR CI -- gh pr checks exits non-zero (code 8) while any check is still pending, which breaks naive `until <cmd>; do sleep; done` polling patterns built around the command's own exit code or grep on its output.
deadEnds: DEAD-END: a hand-rolled `until gh pr checks 655 | grep -qv 'pending\|queued\|in_progress'; do sleep 20; done` loop is wrong -- it exits as soon as ANY single check stops being pending, not when ALL checks conclude, because grep -v matches on any line that lacks those substrings regardless of the other lines' state. Replaced with `gh pr checks --watch`, built for exactly this.
